title: Who came up with that requirement?
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Think of a rule you follow at work or in life that you have never explained. Who made it? Why?
Jose explained an idea he calls cognitive entrenchment. It is a tendency to get stuck in a particular way of thinking when the evidence suggests otherwise.

As Jose describes it from the book, there was a government requirement for the founder's rockets. The engineers' natural answer was no, we can't, there is a requirement. The founder asked: who came up with that requirement? He challenged it even though, quote unquote, it was the law.
Jose said the way we are educated makes us specialized. Information is chunked so that people can memorize it and apply it.
There is a saying, he said: if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.
He added that engineers train with very rigid, structured systems, so getting them out of that is sometimes a challenge.

groups.heading: What is the skill set he is using?

lines.text: So what skill is the founder using, Jose asked, to lead people when he has no deep experience in what they do?
A student said: contrarian thinking. Another said he brings everything back to first principles, the basic laws you don't need deep knowledge to understand. Jose said both are right.

Then Jose gave his example. You go to a mechanic and you know nothing about engines. He could charge you five hundred dollars, or two thousand. Your lack of knowledge is a threat. So you have to challenge what the mechanic is doing. What resource do you use?

His answer, about the founder: he is looking for bias. He studies the person and asks how that person is limited in their way of thinking. It is more a study of the human's limitation than of the subject.
Jose asked if there was another way to explain it. A student said the founder is like a sponge, learning on the go from the people who know. Jose agreed that was another concept.

Jose gave one more example from the book. As he describes it, the founder looked at the thickness of the steel and asked: why can't it be 4? Why does it have to be 16? The engineers said that was too scary: below 4, they were not comfortable. He said okay, we will stop there, make it 4, but he pushed them to get rid of the bias in those government requirements.
Jose added: of course there is a risk tolerance to this. You have to know your risk tolerance, and be comfortable with it.

groups.heading: Who came up with that requirement?

lines.text: Which rule do you follow without knowing who made it?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Pick one rule you follow at work or in life without knowing who made it.
Write: who came up with it, and is it still true?
Write what evidence you have that it still works.
Think of one person you rely on for something you do not understand. Write one question that tests how they think, not only what they know.
Write what could go wrong if you broke the rule, and whether you could survive it.

check.q: What does Jose say cognitive entrenchment is?
choices: Getting stuck in one way of thinking when the evidence suggests otherwise
Disliking change in other people only

check.q: To challenge a mechanic about something you know nothing about, what does Jose say to study?
choices: How the person is limited in their way of thinking

check.q: Which saying did Jose use about being over-specialized?
choices: If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail
A stitch in time saves nine

recap: Smart people get stuck in the way they were taught. Ask who came up with the rule, and study how a person thinks.
